title: Delegates and lambdas
summary: Store a method in a variable, pass it as an argument, and write small functions inline.

steps.title: A method as a value
body: Say you need the orders over 100, then the orders from one customer, then the unpaid ones. The loop is the same each time. Only the *test* changes.
A **delegate** is a type whose values are methods. It lets you pass the test in as an argument. C# has three ready-made families:
| Type | Holds a method that | Example |
| `Func<int, bool>` | takes an `int`, returns a `bool` | "is it even?" |
| `Func<string, string, int>` | takes two strings, returns an `int` | "compare these" |
| `Action<string>` | takes a `string`, returns nothing | "print this" |
| `Predicate<int>` | takes an `int`, returns a `bool` | an older name for `Func<int, bool>` |
For `Func`, the **last** type argument is the return type. `Action` never returns anything.
The quickest way to make a value for a delegate is a **lambda**: parameters, `=>`, then the result.
```csharp
Func<int, bool> isEven = n => n % 2 == 0;
Console.WriteLine(isEven(4));   // True - call it like a method

steps.prompt: Match each delegate type to a lambda it can hold.
steps.explain: Count the parameters on the left of `=>`, then look at what the right side produces. For `Func` the last type argument is the result; `Action` has no result.

code: Func<int, int, int> add = (a, b) => a + b;
steps.explain: `add(3, 4)` is 7, and `twice(7)` is 14. A delegate variable is called exactly like a method.

steps.title: Lambda syntax
body: A lambda comes in a few shapes. They all mean "a small method without a name".
```csharp
Func<int, int> square = x => x * x;              // one parameter, one expression
Func<int, int, int> add = (a, b) => a + b;        // several parameters need ( )
Func<string> greet = () => "hello";               // no parameters: empty ( )
Action<string> log = msg => Console.WriteLine(msg);
Func<int, string> grade = score =>                // several statements need { } and return
if (score >= 50) return "pass";
return "fail";
The parameter types are not written. The compiler takes them from the delegate type on the left.
The real power: a method can take a delegate as a **parameter**.
```csharp
static int CountWhere(List<int> items, Func<int, bool> test)
int count = 0;
foreach (int item in items)
if (test(item)) count++;
return count;
int big = CountWhere(totals, t => t > 100);

steps.prompt: Complete the two delegates. `length` returns how long a string is. `shout` prints a string in capitals.
steps.explain: `s.Length` is an `int`, so the last type argument of the `Func` is `int`. `shout` returns nothing, so it is an `Action`. `Func<string>` would mean "takes nothing, returns a string".

steps.title: Filter and Map
prompt: Write the two most useful higher-order methods there are. Both are generic and both take a delegate.
- `static List<T> Filter<T>(List<T> items, Func<T, bool> keep)` returns a new list with only the items for which `keep` returns `true`, in the same order.
- `static List<TOut> Map<TIn, TOut>(List<TIn> items, Func<TIn, TOut> convert)` returns a new list with `convert` applied to every item.
Write the loops yourself. In the next lesson you will meet the built-in versions.
starter: static List<T> Filter<T>(List<T> items, Func<T, bool> keep)
// add each item that passes the test
static List<TOut> Map<TIn, TOut>(List<TIn> items, Func<TIn, TOut> convert)
// add the converted version of each item
solution: static List<T> Filter<T>(List<T> items, Func<T, bool> keep)
static List<TOut> Map<TIn, TOut>(List<TIn> items, Func<TIn, TOut> convert)
template: Dojo.Eq("Filter keeps totals over 100", new List<int> { 120, 300 }, Filter(totals, t => t > 100));
Dojo.Eq("Filter with a test nothing passes is empty", new List<int>(), Filter(totals, t => t > 1000));
Dojo.Eq("Filter works on strings", new List<string> { "mug" }, Filter(new List<string> { "tea", "mug" }, s => s.StartsWith("m")));
Dojo.Eq("Map doubles every total", new List<int> { 10, 240, 160, 600 }, Map(totals, t => t * 2));
Dojo.Eq("Map can change the type: string to int", new List<int> { 3, 6 }, Map(new List<string> { "tea", "teapot" }, s => s.Length));
Dojo.Eq("the original list is unchanged", new List<int> { 5, 120, 80, 300 }, totals);

forbid.message: Uses its own loop, not a built-in

hints: Loop over `items` with `foreach`. A delegate parameter is called like a method: `keep(item)`.
`Map`: `result.Add(convert(item));` The loop variable has type `TIn`; what you add has type `TOut`.

steps.title: Closures
body: A lambda can use variables from the code around it. This is called **capturing**, and a lambda that does it is a **closure**.
```csharp
int minimum = 100;
Func<int, bool> isBig = total => total > minimum;   // uses minimum from outside
That is what makes lambdas so handy: the test can depend on user input or a method parameter.
The catch: the lambda captures the **variable**, not a copy of its value. It reads the variable at the moment it *runs*, not at the moment it was written.
```csharp
minimum = 500;
Console.WriteLine(isBig(200));   // False - it sees the new value

code: Func<int, bool> isBig = n => n > threshold;
steps.explain: The lambda holds on to the variable `threshold` itself. When it runs the second time, `threshold` is 20, so `15 > 20` is false.

steps.prompt: The same rule causes a famous bug. What does this print?
steps.explain: A `for` loop has **one** variable `i` for the whole loop. All three lambdas capture that same variable. They run after the loop has ended, when `i` is 3. The fix is to copy the value into a new variable inside the loop body: `int copy = i;` and capture `copy`. (`foreach` does not have this problem: its variable is new on every pass.)

steps.title: Method groups
body: If a method already exists with the right shape, you do not need to wrap it in a lambda. Pass its **name**, with no parentheses. This is called a **method group**.
```csharp
static bool IsOverdue(Invoice invoice) => invoice.DaysLate > 0;
var a = Filter(invoices, invoice => IsOverdue(invoice));   // works
var b = Filter(invoices, IsOverdue);                       // same thing, shorter
names.ForEach(Console.WriteLine);                          // prints every name
`IsOverdue` with no `()` means "the method itself". `IsOverdue(x)` means "call it now and use the result".

steps.prompt: Which delegate type fits each lambda?
steps.explain: `Func<int, bool>` takes an `int` and gives back a `bool`. `Action<int>` takes an `int` and gives back nothing. `Func<int>` takes nothing and gives back an `int`.

steps.title: The captured loop variable
prompt: `MakeMultipliers(3)` should return three functions: one that multiplies by 1, one by 2, one by 3.
Right now every function multiplies by 4. Run it, work out why, and fix it. Keep the `for` loop.
hints: All the lambdas share the one variable `i`. By the time any of them runs, the loop has finished and `i` is `count + 1`.
Each pass through the loop body needs its *own* variable for the lambda to capture.
Inside the loop body, before `result.Add`, write `int factor = i;` and use `factor` in the lambda.
